bibl.title: Time scales of memory, learning, and plasticity

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The strategy of the nervous system to overcome these limitations apparently is to use different time scales in the memorization process.

span.label: time scales of memory, learning, and synaptic plasticity
span.quote: Psychology and physiology have found and described many different memory mechanisms, and these mechanisms indeed use different time scales.

span.label: review
span.quote: In this prospect we review these mechanisms with respect to their time scale and propose relations between mechanisms in learning and memory and their underlying physiological basis.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Forgetting on finite, graded storage times acts as an implicit compression algorithm, holding down both the capacity needed and the time to retrieve an item
span.quote: Hence, the nervous system is implicitly performing an algorithm by means of its finite storage time (i.e., by forgetting meaningless items) to more efficiently store and access data.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: New memories overwrite and interfere with old ones, which lowers the network's capacity demand but destroys important items - the cost that multiple time scales exist to avoid
span.quote: Another possibility is the permanent overwriting or interference with old memories, which in turn reduces the capacity requirements of the network [see, e.g., (Mézard et al. 1986; Sikström 2002) for Hopfield models] but also deletes important memories.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Hebbian potentiation feeds back on itself - a strengthened synapse drives the postsynaptic neuron harder, which strengthens it further - producing runaway weight growth unless a counteracting mechanism is present
span.quote: Independently of the interpretation of Hebbian plasticity this mechanism results in divergent dynamics: if an input drives the firing of a postsynaptic neuron, then plasticity potentiates the synaptic weight and, in this way, causes a stronger input drive, which in turn generates more potentiation, and so on.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An organism evolves a given memory time scale only if its lifespan and environment exert evolutionary pressure for correlations at that scale
span.quote: For example, an organism that lives only for a few weeks will never “feel” the evolutionary pressure to develop long-term memories for planning food harvesting for the winter season.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Spike-triggered calcium influx into the presynaptic terminal raises release probability (facilitation) while use depletes the vesicle pool (depression), giving synapses a seconds-long memory
span.quote: The arrival of spikes at the synapse leads to a calcium influx into the presynaptic terminal and, thus, to an increase in the release probability (synaptic facilitation).

span.label: The review is selective rather than exhaustive; only key findings are discussed for each link.
span.quote: To avoid this, only key findings are discussed.

span.label: The mapping from physiological mechanism to behaviour is not established, so the links presented are possibilities rather than established correspondences.
span.quote: Because it is not clear which mechanism is responsible for which behavior, we discussed possible links.

span.label: Only links with existing experimental or modelling support are treated; missing links are flagged as open questions rather than covered.
span.quote: Up to this point we have only discussed links for which there is already experimental support or theoretical modeling.

span.label: The review's two neighbouring memory categories are given non-overlapping time ranges.
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: The ordering between the two categories is stated to be unresolved and posed as a question.
span.quote: The interaction between short- and long-term memory remains unclear (McGaugh 2000). Does a memory item have to be stored in short-term memory before it is transferred to longterm memory

span.label: A construct used throughout the learning-algorithm literature has no established physiology for its longer form.
span.quote: These so-called eligibility traces (Hull 1943; Rall 1967) are used in many approaches [e.g., Sutton (1988); Sutton and Barto (1998); Suri and Schultz (1999); Porr and Wörgötter (2003)] to bridge time gaps in learning algorithms, but the physiological basis of longer traces is unclear

span.label: working memory
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: short-term memory
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: long-term memory
span.quote: Although the time scale of long-term memory could be up to “infinity,” it is still under debate how items can be stored for such a long time

span.label: eligibility traces
span.quote: These so-called eligibility traces (Hull 1943; Rall 1967) are used in many approaches [e.g., Sutton (1988); Sutton and Barto (1998); Suri and Schultz (1999); Porr and Wörgötter (2003)] to bridge time gaps in learning algorithms, but the physiological basis of longer traces is unclear

span.label: time scale
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: consolidation → retrieval
span.note: THE TWO CANNOT BE SEPARATED IN THIS STUDY - the DESIGN form of the negative relation (Q-286/Q-287). No edge type can express it: all eight assert that a relation HOLDS. Recorded here because a confounding statement BOUNDS WHAT THE PAPER'S OWN RESULTS CAN MEAN, and it lives in a methods paragraph where nothing downstream will find it. A memory deficit cannot be attributed to either of the two processes the field distinguishes - so the distinction survives in the vocabulary while being unusable on the data.
span.quote: However, it is difficult to investigate consolidation in memory recall because for memory deficits it cannot be distinguished between a loss in consolidation or a loss in retrieval (Dudai 2004).

span.label: a time scale - THREE DIFFERENT SPANS UNDER ONE EXPRESSION: working memory milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory minutes to days, long-term memory up to what the authors put in scare quotes as 'infinity'; the phrase that organises the whole review denotes a different quantity in each of its three sections
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: long-term memory's upper bound - IN THE AUTHORS' OWN SCARE QUOTES: given as up to 'infinity', with the immediate qualification that it is still under debate how items can be stored for such a long time, so the widest value in the review is the one marked as least settled
span.quote: Although the time scale of long-term memory could be up to “infinity,” it is still under debate how items can be stored for such a long time

span.label: an eligibility trace - A MODELLING DEVICE WITHOUT ITS PHYSIOLOGY: named in 1943 and used in many learning-algorithm approaches to bridge time gaps, while the physiological basis of the longer traces is stated to be unclear, so the algorithms assume a mechanism the review declines to underwrite
span.quote: These so-called eligibility traces (Hull 1943; Rall 1967) are used in many approaches [e.g., Sutton (1988); Sutton and Barto (1998); Suri and Schultz (1999); Porr and Wörgötter (2003)] to bridge time gaps in learning algorithms, but the physiological basis of longer traces is unclear

span.label: builds-on → Martin et al. (2000) four criteria for relating plasticity to learning and memory
span.quote: Nevertheless, to guarantee the correctness of these links, all of them must be tested according to the four criteria proposed by Martin et al. (2000) (detectability, mimicry, and anterograde and retrograde alteration).

span.label: contradicts → Hebb (1949) proposed link between long-term memory and long-term plasticity
span.quote: In summary, it is interesting to note that there exist experimental support for links between (1) working memory and activity and (2) long-term memory and structural plasticity, but the very early proposed link between long-term memory and long-term plasticity (Hebb 1949) is still under debate

span.label: working memory —contrasted-with→ short-term memory
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days

span.label: The three memory concepts occupy non-overlapping time scales: working memory spans milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory minutes to days, and long-term memory days to years.
span.quote: Whereas the time scale of working memory is from milliseconds to minutes, short-term memory stores items on a time scale of minutes to days.

span.label: Having several distinct storage time scales, rather than one, protects important memories from being erased by the overwriting and interference that ongoing storage would otherwise cause.
span.quote: Thus, different time scales could avoid the deletion of important information.

span.label: Robot experiments in which a fast adaptation process is combined with a slow one produce more complex behaviour than either time scale alone.
span.quote: Furthermore, if different time scales interact, then one observes in robot experiments that more complex behaviors can be obtained.

span.label: Caenorhabditis elegans shows synaptic plasticity but no experience-based structural plasticity, so organisms do not necessarily exploit all available time scales.
span.quote: For example, no experiencebased structural plasticity [(Chen et al. 2006; Varshney et al. 2011), long time scale] was found in the “simple” worm Caenorhabditis elegans, while it can still make use of synaptic plasticity [(Dabbish and Raizen 2011), shorter time scale].

span.label: Of the proposed memory-physiology links, working memory-to-activity and long-term-memory-to-structural-plasticity have experimental support, whereas the classic long-term-memory-to-long-term-plasticity link is still disputed.
span.quote: In summary, it is interesting to note that there exist experimental support for links between (1) working memory and activity and (2) long-term memory and structural plasticity, but the very early proposed link between long-term memory and long-term plasticity (Hebb 1949) is still under debate

span.label: Of Martin et al.'s four criteria for tying plasticity to memory, mimicry has never been experimentally realised.
span.quote: So far, mimicry cannot be experimentally induced.

span.label: Rats in enriched environments grow significantly more dendritic spines than controls, which the authors read as experimental evidence linking long-term memory to structural plasticity.
span.quote: When rats experience enriched environments, their dendrites start to build significantly more spines than in a control environment (Xu et al. 2009; Yang et al. 2009).

span.label: Adding synaptic scaling with a quadratic weight dependence to a generic plasticity rule can be shown mathematically to stabilise weight development.
span.quote: It can be shown mathematically that adding synaptic scaling with quadratic weight dependence to generic plasticity rules stabilizes weight development (Tetzlaff et al. 2011).

span.label: Structural plasticity is modelled only computationally because no analytical models of network topology change exist yet.
span.quote: One reason is that analytical models of topological changes in networks have not yet been developed.

span.label: Whether the exact human forgetting curve is exponential or a power law remains unsettled.
span.quote: The exact shape of this forgetting curve is still under debate [exponential or power law; (Wixted and Ebbesen 1991; Anderson and Tweney 1997)].

span.label: working memory
span.quote: Working memory, a term coined by Miller et al. (1960), is a theoretical concept believed to underlie human thought processes.

span.label: long-term memory
span.quote: The memory type with the longest time scale is long-term memory, which operates on a scale of days to years—perhaps even for an entire lifetime.

span.label: chunking
span.quote: Note that this capacity might be increased by a process called chunking, whereby atomic information is combined into larger compounds, with the chunks being stored somewhere else.

span.label: detectability (criterion linking plasticity to memory)
span.quote: Detectability means that there are changes at the synaptic level after an animal has learned or memorized something (e.g., Rioult-Pedotti et al., 1998; Whitlock et al., 2006).

span.label: retrograde alteration
span.quote: Retrograde alteration implies varying the synaptic strength in such a way that a learned memory item can be “reprogrammed” to become another memory (Pastalkova et al. 2006).

span.label: structural plasticity
span.quote: Beside synaptic plasticity, which adapts the synaptic strength between neurons, structural plasticity decides which synapse is created and which is deleted (Holtmaat and Svoboda 2009; Caroni et al. 2012).

span.label: eligibility traces
span.quote: These so-called eligibility traces (Hull 1943; Rall 1967) are used in many approaches [e.g., Sutton (1988); Sutton and Barto (1998); Suri and Schultz (1999); Porr and Wörgötter (2003)] to bridge time gaps in learning algorithms, but the physiological basis of longer traces is unclear.

span.label: intrinsic plasticity
span.quote: Intrinsic plasticity (Triesch 2007; Mozzachiodi and Byrne 2009; Gründemann and Häusser 2010) describes a mechanism that changes, based on the neuron’s activity history, a neuron’s input–output activity relation, thereby leading to distinct neuronal responses for different “memorized” activities.

span.label: synaptic tagging
span.quote: Here, highly active synapses are tagged for long-lasting potentiation.

span.label: reservoir computing
span.quote: The abstract idea of this concept is that a complex network of calculating identities (e.g., neurons) is so diverse that each task is solved somewhere within the network (Maass et al. 2002; Buonomano and Maass 2009; Maass 2010).

span.label: synaptic scaling
span.quote: Here, the synaptic efficiency of all inputs to a neuron increases/ decreases if the activity of this neuron is lower/higher than a target activity (Davis 2006).

span.label: about 10 days — how quickly the nervous system's storage capacity would be exhausted if every bit of input were stored
span.quote: If we stored every bit of input, capacity of our nervous system would be reached after only about 10 days.

span.label: four and seven — the number of items working memory can hold
span.quote: An important feature of working memory is that it has an individually limited capacity between four and seven storable items

span.label: tens of milliseconds — the time scale of the postsynaptic potential, the shortest memory-like physiological trace
span.quote: The time scale of PSPs is on the order of tens of milliseconds.

span.label: μ = 0.01 corresponds to 100 ms — how the alpha-function time-scale parameter maps onto the filter's temporal duration
span.quote: Here, the time scale parameter μ directly relates to the temporal duration of the filter (e.g., μ = 0.01 corresponds to 100 ms).

span.label: four — the number of criteria Martin et al. proposed for establishing that plasticity underlies learning and memory (detectability, mimicry, anterograde and retrograde alteration)
span.quote: In 2000, Martin et al. in a review suggested four different criteria supporting the hypothesis that plasticity is the basic mechanism for learning and memory: detectability, mimicry, anterograde, and retrograde alteration (Martin et al., 2000; Martin and Morris, 2002).

span.label: milliseconds to seconds — the time scale of short-term plasticity
span.quote: An experimentally well-established physiological theory is short-term plasticity (Markram et al. 1998), which has a time scale of milliseconds to seconds.

span.label: hours to several days — the time scale on which structural plasticity rewires the network
span.quote: The time scale of these changes is from hours to several days.
